docs.x: We ran Cryo against the scheduled Spark jobs teams usually write for themselves, on real Iceberg tables, with three trials per test and every row checked afterwards. Here is what we measured.

The real alternative to Cryo is usually not another product. It is a Spark job on a schedule that someone on the team wrote and now has to maintain. So that is what we measured Cryo against, using the same Spark and Iceberg versions and the same cluster. No maintenance The table as ingestion leaves it. Sets the baseline. Scheduled Spark DAG Compact, rewrite manifests and expire snapshots on every table, every cycle.

docs.h: It touches only the tables that need work
docs.x: We gave both approaches the same fleet: healthy tables, quiet ones, fragmenting ones, badly fragmented ones, and tables taking row updates. Over four cycles, the scheduled DAG rewrote everything it saw. Cryo left healthy tables alone and spent its work where the problems were. Green chips are rewrites that fixed a real problem. Orange chips rewrote a table that was already healthy. Both approaches expire snapshots on
Scheduled DAG 48 Cryo 10 Identical in all three trials. Counting snapshot expiry, it is 88 vs 50.
No maintenance 66% Scheduled DAG 100% Cryo 100% Share of query runs that hit a healthy table. Cryo matched the brute-force DAG while doing less of the work nobody needed.

docs.h: On a 100 GiB table, queries get faster
docs.x: One table, 100 GiB, fragmented the way streaming ingestion leaves it. One Cryo run at the default 256 MB target turned thousands of small files into a few hundred right-sized ones. 67 GiB rewritten in one run of about 21 minutes. Same rows and same results, a tenth of the files. Query speed after one Cryo run Scans and aggregates gained the most. Single-row lookups got slower because each one now opens a larger file;
128, 256 and 512 MB targets all landed in this range for the whole query mix. The default is a safe choice. 690 = 690
Cryo's compaction produced exactly the same file count, bytes and results as an engineer running the same SQL by hand. 538 – 802

docs.h: Queries to pay back the rewrite
docs.x: Customer filters repaid the compaction compute after 538 runs, whole-table aggregates after 588 and full reads after 802.

docs.h: Under live CDC, it keeps up
docs.x: This is the case that breaks naive schedules. A MERGE landed on the table every 200 seconds for two hours. The scheduled DAG's compactions collided with the writer and failed every time. Cryo converted delete files in small commits between writes and kept the table lean. No maintenance Scheduled Spark DAG Cryo The no-maintenance and scheduled-DAG lines overlap because the DAG's work never committed. Ticks along the b
Every job finished while the writer kept committing. 0 / 3
All three failed validation against the concurrent MERGE. 40 → 3
Same rows, and aggregate queries ran in 0.58× the time.

We ran a steady stream of dashboard-style queries against the 100 GiB table while Cryo rewrote 67 GiB of it, then compared with the same queries on an idle table. Idle table During Cryo compaction p95 stayed within 0.88× to 1.04× of idle across every query, and p99 improved for all three. Zero query failures.

It starts one Spark application per operation and expires snapshots on every table. Compute is cheap next to engineer time, but Cryo is not a compute saver. A maintenance run compacts first, then cleans up, in one fixed order. The order is defined in code and no preset can change it.

Seven operations, skipping the ones a table does not need. Expiry comes after compaction so one run reclaims the space its own compaction freed. Compact convert_deletes Rewrites data files so delete files are applied and no longer re-merged on every read. rewrite_position_deletes Consolidates position-delete files without rewriting data. Spark only. optimize Partition-aware compaction of small files, planned from sto

Apache Iceberg gives you hidden partitioning, snapshot isolation, schema evolution and engine-agnostic metadata. It does not promise that tables stay fast. Left alone, four things pile up, and each one compounds independently, so fixing one does not fix the others. Rewrites data files so delete files are applied and no longer re-merged on every read. On Spark it passes a delete-file threshold. On Trino it runs as an OPTIMIZE .
Consolidates position-delete files without rewriting data. Spark only, because Trino does not support it.
Partition-aware compaction of small files, planned from stored scan data. This is the step the chunking rules below exist to protect.
Refreshes table statistics straight after compaction, while the new layout is fresh.
Consolidates manifests. Trino calls it optimize_manifests and Spark calls it rewrite_manifests .
Drops snapshots the retention policy would not keep, and the files only they referenced. Guarded, and forcing it is audited.
Deletes files in storage that no snapshot references. Guarded, and forcing it is audited.

A large table is never compacted in one statement. The planner ranks partitions by small-file count, highest first, skips those under the min_small_files threshold, and then picks one of three paths. The scanner grades a table from stored metadata. It does not scan data files on the request path, and object storage is not an input.

Every table starts at 100 points and loses points for each problem the scan finds. The grade is the letter for the final score. The home chart counts tables per grade. It is not a size-weighted median. UI words map to letters: A Excellent, B Good, C Fair, D Poor, F Critical. The planner is engine-agnostic. Trino SQL and Spark SQL are rendered apart, so the same plan produces different SQL and never different intent.

Every operation in the canonical order has a renderer for each engine, with one exception: rewrite_position_deletes is Spark only today.
